Every prime number greater than 2 is odd.why: Stated directly on Wikipedia and, in its equivalent form '2 is the only even prime', thousands of times in Dolma.

sources.quote: Therefore, every prime number other than 2 is an odd number, and is called an odd prime.

sources.query: all primes greater than 2 are odd
prime number greater than 2 is odd

The newly discovered prime Q, which has.why: An unnamed new prime: its parity is never written down; the rule (or its equivalent, 2 is the only even prime) gives it.

sources.query: prime number with millions of digits

A prime number p greater than 2 leaves a.why: The remainder of an unnamed prime is worked out from its parity, which comes from the rule.

sources.query: remainder when p is divided by 2
p divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 1

sources.note: The usual way proofs introduce an odd prime: an assumption about p, not the remainder asked here.

A prime number of marbles greater than 2.why: A word problem no text contains: the parity of the count comes from the rule, and an even count splits evenly.

sources.query: marbles AND prime number greater than 2

A right angle measures 90 degrees..why: The definition of a right angle, the first sentence of its Wikipedia article.

sources.quote: In geometry and trigonometry, a right angle is an angle of exactly 90 degrees or π/2 radians corresponding to a quarter turn.

9 is a prime number..why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: 9 = 3 × 3 is composite.

sources.quote: 9 is the fourth composite number, the first odd composite number, a square, a Motzkin number, and the number of derangements of 4 items.

notes: TBox contraction paired with mathematics-replace-0007: removes 'every prime number greater than 2 is odd'. The derived queries reuse the revision's new members (a newly discovered prime Q, a prime p greater than 2, a bag with a prime number of marbles), each stated in the prompt. The near query (is 2 a prime) shares the subject and does not follow from the rule.
